segments.text: Good morning, Mrs Pell. I've got the letter from your last visit open in front of me, the one about the puffy ankles and the tablets. And Marisol, lovely to see you as well.
Morning, doctor. Sorry, we're a bit flustered, the taxi came early and she has asked me three times whether we left the oven on.
I haven't asked three times. Twice. Well, perhaps three. Anyway, doctor, it's these dizzy spells that bother me, that's why we've come.
Right, let's start with the dizzy spells. When do they come on?
Mostly when I get up out of the chair. The room goes all swimmy and I have to hold on to the table until it passes.
And how long has that been going on?
Oh, a fortnight. No, longer than that. Two weeks, three weeks, I think, it was before my last appointment at the hairdresser's anyway.
It's three weeks, doctor. I wrote it on the calendar the day she nearly went over in the kitchen.
Goodness. Is it any particular time of day, or does it pick its moments?
Most mornings, and once after lunch. It's never in the evenings, is it, Marisol? Or was that Tuesday?
You said the hairdresser's, do you still go to Maureen's? Last time you told me she'd done half the street's weddings.
Every other Friday, and she's seventy-eight and still going. I was a teacher for forty years, you know, and half her customers are my old pupils' mothers.
What a wonderful thing. Now, the ankles. When I saw you they were quite puffy, how are they?
The swelling in my ankles has gone, hasn't it, Marisol? I can get my slippers on again without a shoehorn.
Yes, since the second week they've been fine. It's the dizziness and honestly the tablets I'm worried about.
Tell me about the tablets then. What is she taking at the moment?
The amlodipine, five milligrams every morning for her blood pressure. And paracetamol, the 500 milligram ones, when she needs them for the arthritis.
I've had the high blood pressure since I was fifty. And the arthritis is in my hands mostly, that's why I can't manage the childproof lids.
And the mix-ups with the tablets, Marisol? You mentioned something to the receptionist on the phone.
Twice last week she'd had the morning tablet by lunchtime and then said she hadn't, so I nearly gave her another. I caught it once. The other time I honestly don't know.
I didn't take two. Did I? I did put the little box back in the wrong drawer, that I do know.
Those little boxes wander off, don't they? Marisol, you sound worn out. Do you look after her day and night?
I live in, so yes. I'm up with her at night, and since my sister couldn't come this month I haven't had a day off. I'm tired, doctor, that's all.
That's a lot to carry, and it matters for her safety too, so we'll talk about it before you leave. Mrs Pell, do you manage at home all right, with the flat?
It's my own flat, I've been in it since 1974, and Marisol has the little back room now. I wouldn't live anywhere else.
And I won't ask what you get up to on a Friday night, but do you still enjoy your sherry?
One glass on a Sunday, that's the only drink I have all week. Don't look at me like that, Marisol.
Lovely. Now let me take a look at you. Sit forward for me, and take a few breaths in through your nose.
Is this far enough? My back doesn't like the stool.
Your chest sounds clear, and there's no swelling in either ankle now. Nice and slim, those ankles.
Any trouble with your breathing, or with your chest when you get dizzy?
No, my breathing is fine. I walked up the path with the stick and I wasn't puffed at all.

Good. Here's my thinking. I can't rule out your blood pressure dropping when you stand up, and the morning tablet going in twice on some days could be adding to it. I'm not going to guess beyond that today.
So what do we do about it?
I'd like to arrange a blood test today, and an ECG, a tracing of the heart, before you leave the building. Both are quick, and the nurse down the hall will do them.
Will it hurt? I hated the needle last time, I went white as a sheet.
Just a small scratch, and you can lie down for it. And Marisol, a weekly pill organiser would help, you fill it on Sunday and the old boxes go in a locked drawer.
Yes, I can do that. Thank you, I feel a bit less alone with it now.
You are not on your own. Mind the step on the way out, Mrs Pell, and Marisol, do take a proper afternoon off when your sister comes.
